      <title>Interest rates unlikely to reach 4.75% by next summer, say City economists</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/25/interest-rates-bank-of-england-rises-summer-2027</link>
      <description><p>Experts say Bank of England  unlikely to increase rates by full percentage point – and could lower them by end of 2027</p><p>Financial markets are wrong to predict the Bank of England will raise UK interest rates by a full percentage point or more by next summer, City economists believe.</p><p>According to market-implied interest rate expectations, the Bank is likely to raise interest rates at least four times over the next year, lifting the bank rate from <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/sep/17/bank-of-england-holds-interest-rates-inflation">3.75% today</a> to 4.75% by the end of July, and possibly to 5% – meaning five rises – by December 2027.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/25/interest-rates-bank-of-england-rises-summer-2027">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/23/hammersmith-bridge-crumbling-traffic-delays-roadworks-london</link>
      <description><p>London’s roads are horrendous, with constant roadworks and creaking infrastructure. And the emblem of all that spans the River Thames</p><p>London’s Hammersmith Bridge is a metaphor for all that is wrong with British government. Closed to motor traffic and inert for seven years, it is a victim of the anarchy that seeps into every tier of public administration. The bridge sits today on a sublime bend in the Thames, guarded by what looks like Checkpoint Charlie in iron curtain Berlin. With Albert Bridge also <a href="https://www.rbkc.gov.uk/streets-and-transport/albert-bridge-repairs">now closed</a>, 37,000 extra vehicles seeking to cross the river have brought south London close to perpetual gridlock. No one cares.</p><p>London may be the richest, smartest, coolest place in Britain. Yet it is run like a high street vape shop.       <description><p>The UK still imports 60% of its gas and, even with Jackdaw, its energy supply and resilience problems are not going away</p><p>After the overdue <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/nils-pratley-on-finance/2026/oct/21/jackdaw-approval-step-towards-grownup-north-sea-policy">approval of the Jackdaw field</a> in the North Sea, here comes a reminder that Britain still imports almost 60% of its gas and the stuff has to come from somewhere. We’re now doing a deal with Belgium to ensure enough supply can flow through a connecting pipeline this winter should a “low-probability but high-impact stress event”, to quote the regulatory mouthful, occur.</p><p>To be fair, the arrangement to maintain capacity from Belgium is a belt-and-braces measure. The imagined events do sound genuinely stressful and may never happen. A critical piece of infrastructure, such as the two import terminals in Milford Haven to bring in liquefied natural gas (LNG) into Britain, would have to be out of action during a prolonged cold snap in which demand is very high.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/nils-pratley-on-finance/2026/oct/23/britains-gas-security-needs-reinforcement-last-minute-deals-with-belgium-are-not-a-proper-fix">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Our economy needs it. The NHS needs it. And making foreign workers’ lives more miserable – as the home secretary plans to do – will undermine integration</p><p>My mum’s carer was uncharacteristically late one morning. She didn’t want to say why at first, but it turned out she’d found her previous client – an elderly lady living all alone, with no family to visit – collapsed on the floor, barely alive. It was a lot to cope with for someone only in their early 20s, a reminder of the heavy responsibility this job carries. Watching the carers who helped both my parents in their respective final weeks taught me that while the work itself might seem mundane, the emotional and social skills needed to do it well – to coax some sense out of the confused, to jolly along the lonely, and to soothe the dying, to walk in and out of unfamiliar houses all day long without quite knowing what you might find – are anything but.</p><p>Yet like so many jobs predominantly done by women, care has long been relentlessly undervalued. That means lousy pay, little public recognition, and now – at least for the disproportionately large chunk of this workforce who are migrant workers – the disorientating realisation that the government can snap its fingers and all your life plans are upended overnight.</p><p>Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/oct/23/labour-truth-immigration-economy-nhs-home-secretary">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/oct/21/a-plan-to-ensure-energy-is-affordable-for-all</link>
      <description><p><strong>Dr Alex Chapman </strong>calls for a government-funded price cap on an essential block of electricity and gas, in response to an article by Nils Pratley </p><p>Nils Pratley thinks that the secretary of state, Miatta Fahnbulleh, should “keep things simple” and develop a targeted social tariff to protect vulnerable households from surging energy bills (<a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/nils-pratley-on-finance/2026/oct/14/the-uk-energy-secretary-is-flirting-with-a-bad-idea-for-bills-the-rising-block-tariff">The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff, 14 October</a>). Unfortunately, there is nothing simple about such&nbsp;a&nbsp;scheme.</p><p>Pratley’s proposal would mean creating a new benefits system inside our privatised energy industry. If the interminable debates about our current benefits system were not enough to put him off, we can look to the failing social care system to see where it might lead. Andy Burnham has made it his life’s mission to dismantle this lottery that can strip pensioners of their savings and the family home. Just as he now plans a universal public provision of adult social care, we at the New&nbsp;Economics Foundation have such a plan for energy.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/oct/21/a-plan-to-ensure-energy-is-affordable-for-all">Continue reading...</a></description>
